idiom_name: implicitly satisfied interface stored in a struct field
implementation_notes: Go has no implements clause: a type satisfies the implementor interface by having the methods, so the abstraction's field is just an interface-typed value and the two sides are decoupled without importing each other. That is the language's replacement for the whole implementor base class - the standard library's one-method io.Reader and io.Writer connect files, sockets, buffers and compressors with no shared ancestry. The idiomatic refinement is to define the interface where it is consumed and to accept interfaces while returning concrete types, which keeps the primitive set minimal. The classic form (an abstract base with a subclass per combination) is not expressible and not needed; for a closed set of implementors in one dispatch site, prefer calling the interface method over a type switch.
pitfalls: A nil interface is not a nil implementation: an interface value holding a typed nil pointer is non-nil, so if s.renderer == nil misses it and the call panics - the classic Go interface trap.
Method sets decide satisfaction: a pointer-receiver method means only *T implements the interface, so storing a value where the abstraction expects the interface fails to compile.

Wide interfaces defeat the decoupling (every implementor and every test fake must implement every method); keep the implementor interface at the primitives actually used and define it next to its consumer.
